# random_ratio in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.10/fn.random_ratio.html

**crate feature**only.

`thread_rng`## Expand description

Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator` of being
true.

That is, `random_ratio(2, 3)` has chance of 2 in 3, or about 67%, of
returning true. If `numerator == denominator`, then the returned value
is guaranteed to be `true`. If `numerator == 0`, then the returned
value is guaranteed to be `false`.

See also the [ Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/distr/struct.Bernoulli.html) distribution, which may be faster if
sampling from the same

`numerator` and `denominator` repeatedly.This function is shorthand for
[rng()](https://docs.rs/fn.rng.html).[random_ratio](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html#method.random_ratio)(`numerator`, `denominator`)

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If `denominator == 0` or `numerator > denominator`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

`println!("{}", rand::random_ratio(2, 3));`

---

# rng in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.10/fn.rng.html

`pub fn rng() -> `[ThreadRng](https://docs.rs/rngs/struct.ThreadRng.html)Available on

**crate feature**only.`thread_rng`## Expand description

Access a fast, pre-initialized generator

This is a handle to the local [ ThreadRng](https://docs.rs/rngs/struct.ThreadRng.html).

See also [ crate::rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html) for alternatives.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
let mut numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
numbers.shuffle(&mut rand::rng());
println!("Numbers: {numbers:?}");
// Using a local binding avoids an initialization-check on each usage:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
println!("True or false: {}", rng.random::<bool>());
println!("A simulated die roll: {}", rng.random_range(1..=6));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

Refer to [ ThreadRng](https://docs.rs/rngs/struct.ThreadRng.html#Security).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This method panics in case of [ SysRng](https://docs.rs/rngs/struct.SysRng.html) failure during initial seeding.

# rand_core 0.10.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1

# rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

## License

The crate is licensed under either of:

at your option.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

# UnwrapErr in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/^0.10/struct.UnwrapErr.html

`pub struct UnwrapErr<R: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)>(pub R);## Expand description

Wrapper around [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) implementation which implements

[by panicking on potential errors.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
fn with_try_rng<R: TryRng>(mut rng: R) {
    // rng does not impl Rng:
    let _ = rng.try_next_u32(); // okay
    // let _ = rng.next_u32(); // error
    // An adapter borrowing rng:
    let _ = UnwrapErr(&mut rng).next_u32();
    // An adapter moving rng:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
fn call_with_unsized_try_rng<R: TryRng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) {
    // R is unsized, thus we must use &mut R:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
```
## Tuple Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.0)

`0: R`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Reborrow with a new lifetime

Rust allows references like `&T` or `&mut T` to be “reborrowed” through
coercion: essentially, the pointer is copied under a new, shorter, lifetime.
Until rfcs#1403 lands, reborrows on user types require a method call.

# TryRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/^0.10/trait.TryRng.html

```
pub trait TryRng {
    type
```
[Error](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Error): [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html);
    // Required methods
    fn [try_next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u32)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u64)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)(&mut self, dst: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.unit.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
}## Expand description

Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

This trait provides a base interface designed to support efficient usage of
(`u32`, `u64`) word generators, block generators and random data sources.
There is no required relationship between the output of each method or any
requirement to use all generated random bits; for example an implementation
of [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) may discard some generated bytes
to avoid storing a partially used word or block.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

[§](https://docs.rs#quality-and-length)Quality and length

Implementions should produce bits uniformly: each output value should be equally likely, without observable patterns in successive outputs or between the output streams of multiple instances of an implementation using different seeds or streams (where supported by the implementation).

Pathological implementations (e.g. constant or counting generators which rarely change some bits) may cause issues in consumers of random data, for example dead-locks in rejection samplers and obviously non-random output (e.g. a counting generator may result in apparently-constant output from a uniform-ranged distribution).

Cryptographically unpredictable output is not a requirement of this trait,
but is a requirement of [ TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html).

In practice, most implementations are pseudo-random number generators with a
finite *period* or *cycle length*, and (among non-cryptographic PRNGs)
statistical anomalies may appear long before a cycle occurs. An
implementation should ensure its period is sufficiently long that no
anomalies are likely to appear in usage and/or document its limitations.

For more on PRNG quality and period, see [The Rust Rand Book: Quality](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#quality).

[§](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)Reproducibility

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes). See also

[The Rust Rand Book: Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Often, usage of the infallible trait [ Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) or its extension trait

[is preferred to direct usage of](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html)

`rand::RngExt``TryRng`.
Many implementations of `TryRng` (those with `type Error = `[Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html))
already implement [; in other cases](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[may be used to obtain an implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.UnwrapErr.html)

`UnwrapErr`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-tryrng)Implementing `TryRng`

Most algorithmic generators (i.e. pseudo-random number generators or PRNGs)
never fail; in this case type `Error` should be [ Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html); in this case
trait

`Rng` is implemented automatically. Cycling is not considered an
error.Small PRNGs often yield either `u32` or `u64` natively.
Module [ crate::utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html) provides utilities to help implement other methods.

Byte sources may implement [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)
natively.
Module

[provides utilities to help implement other methods.](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)

`crate::utils`Block generators (which produce `[u32; N]` or `[u64; N]` for some fixed `N`)
should make use of the [ crate::block](https://docs.rs/block/index.html) module.

With regards to other traits:

- **Do not**implement- `Default`
- **Do**implement- `SeedableRng`- [Reproducibility](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)above.
- Implement `Clone`
- **Do not**implement- `Copy`
- Implement `Debug`
- `Eq`- `PartialEq`

---

# Rng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/^0.10/trait.Rng.html

`pub trait Rng: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)<Error = [Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html)> {
    // Required methods
    fn [next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next_u32)(&mut self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html);
[next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next_u64)(&mut self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html);
[fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.fill_bytes)(&mut self, dst: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]);
}## Expand description

Trait for infallible random number generators

`Rng` is a sub-trait of [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) for infallible generators.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

See [ TryRng#Requirements](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#Requirements) which also apply here.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand/) crate provides higher level functionality, for example
generation of floating-point values, uniform ranged sampling and shuffling
sequences. In particular,

[is an extension trait over](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html)

`rand::RngExt``Rng`
providing many of the methods one might expect to be able to use on an RNG.[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-rng)Implementing `Rng`

# Infallible in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/^0.10/enum.Infallible.html

`pub enum Infallible {}`## Expand description

The error type for errors that can never happen.

Since this enum has no variant, a value of this type can never actually exist.
This can be useful for generic APIs that use [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html) and parameterize the error type,
to indicate that the result is always

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)

`Ok`For example, the [ TryFrom](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html) trait (conversion that returns a

[) has a blanket implementation for all types where a reverse](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[implementation exists.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)

`Into`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T, U> TryFrom<U> for T where U: Into<T> {
    type Error = Infallible;
    fn try_from(value: U) -> Result<Self, Infallible> {
        Ok(U::into(value))  // Never returns `Err`
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#future-compatibility)Future compatibility

This enum has the same role as [the  ! “never” type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.never.html),
which is unstable in this version of Rust.
When

`!` is stabilized, we plan to make `Infallible` a type alias to it:… and eventually deprecate `Infallible`.

However there is one case where `!` syntax can be used
before `!` is stabilized as a full-fledged type: in the position of a function’s return type.
Specifically, it is possible to have implementations for two different function pointer types:

```
trait MyTrait {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> ! {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> std::convert::Infallible {}
```
With `Infallible` being an enum, this code is valid.
However when `Infallible` becomes an alias for the never type,
the two `impl`s will start to overlap
and therefore will be disallowed by the language’s trait coherence rules.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# SeedableRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/^0.10/trait.SeedableRng.html

`pub trait SeedableRng: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    type [Seed](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Seed): [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]> + [AsMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsMut.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]>;
    // Required method
    fn [from_seed](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_seed)(seed: Self::[Seed](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#associatedtype.Seed)) -> Self;
    // Provided methods
    fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self { ... }
[from_rng](https://docs.rs#method.from_rng)<R: [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(rng: [&mut R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)) -> Self { ... }
[try_from_rng](https://docs.rs#method.try_from_rng)<R: [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(rng: [&mut R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, R::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)> { ... }
[fork](https://docs.rs#method.fork)(&mut self) -> Self
       where Self: [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) { ... }
[try_fork](https://docs.rs#method.try_fork)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where Self: [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

This trait encapsulates the low-level functionality common to all pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs, or algorithmic generators).

A generator implementing `SeedableRng` will usually be deterministic, but
beware that portability and reproducibility of results **is not implied**.
Refer to documentation of the generator, noting that generators named after
a specific algorithm are usually tested for reproducibility against a
reference vector, while `SmallRng` and `StdRng` specifically opt out of
reproducibility guarantees.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

Seed type, which is restricted to types mutably-dereferenceable as `u8`
arrays (we recommend `[u8; N]` for some `N`).

It is recommended to seed PRNGs with a seed of at least circa 100 bits,
which means an array of `[u8; 12]` or greater to avoid picking RNGs with
partially overlapping periods.

For cryptographic RNG’s a seed of 256 bits is recommended, `[u8; 32]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-seedablerng-for-rngs-with-large-seeds)Implementing `SeedableRng` for RNGs with large seeds

Note that [ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) is not implemented for large arrays

`[u8; N]` with
`N` > 32. To be able to implement the traits required by `SeedableRng`
for RNGs with such large seeds, the newtype pattern can be used:```
use rand_core::SeedableRng;
const N: usize = 64;
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct MyRngSeed(pub [u8; N]);
pub struct MyRng(MyRngSeed);
impl Default for MyRngSeed {
    fn default() -> MyRngSeed {
        MyRngSeed([0; N])
    }
}
impl AsRef<[u8]> for MyRngSeed {
    fn as_ref(&self) -> &[u8] {
        &self.0
    }
}
impl AsMut<[u8]> for MyRngSeed {
    fn as_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {
        &mut self.0
    }
}
impl SeedableRng for MyRng {
    type Seed = MyRngSeed;
    fn from_seed(seed: MyRngSeed) -> MyRng {
        MyRng(seed)
    }
}
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Create a new PRNG using the given seed.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that bits in the seed are
well distributed. That means usually that the number of one and zero
bits are roughly equal, and values like 0, 1 and (size - 1) are unlikely.
Note that many non-cryptographic PRNGs will show poor quality output
if this is not adhered to. If you wish to seed from simple numbers, use
`seed_from_u64` instead.

All PRNG implementations should be reproducible unless otherwise noted:
given a fixed `seed`, the same sequence of output should be produced
on all runs, library versions and architectures (e.g. check endianness).
Any “value-breaking” changes to the generator should require bumping at
least the minor version and documentation of the change.

It is not required that this function yield the same state as a reference implementation of the PRNG given equivalent seed; if necessary another constructor replicating behaviour from a reference implementation can be added.

PRNG implementations should make sure `from_seed` never panics. In the
case that some special values (like an all zero seed) are not viable
seeds it is preferable to map these to alternative constant value(s),
for example `0xBAD5EEDu32` or `0x0DDB1A5E5BAD5EEDu64` (“odd biases? bad
seed”). This is assuming only a small number of values must be rejected.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/seedable_rng.rs.html#109-121)#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/seedable_rng.rs.html#109-121)

#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

Create a new PRNG using a `u64` seed.

This is a convenience-wrapper around `from_seed` to allow construction
of any `SeedableRng` from a simple `u64` value. It is designed such that
low Hamming Weight numbers like 0 and 1 can be used and should still
result in good, independent seeds to the PRNG which is returned.

This **is not suitable for cryptography**, as should be clear given that
the input size is only 64 bits.

Implementations for PRNGs *may* provide their own implementations of
this function, but the default implementation should be good enough for
all purposes. *Changing* the implementation of this function should be
considered a value-breaking change.

Create a new PRNG seeded from an infallible `Rng`.

This may be useful when needing to rapidly seed many PRNGs from a master PRNG, and to allow forking of PRNGs. It may be considered deterministic.

The master PRNG should be at least as high quality as the child PRNGs.
When seeding non-cryptographic child PRNGs, we recommend using a
different algorithm for the master PRNG (ideally a CSPRNG) to avoid
correlations between the child PRNGs. If this is not possible (e.g.
forking using small non-crypto PRNGs) ensure that your PRNG has a good
mixing function on the output or consider use of a hash function with
`from_seed`.

Note that seeding `XorShiftRng` from another `XorShiftRng` provides an
extreme example of what can go wrong: the new PRNG will be a clone
of the parent.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that a good RNG is provided
for seeding, and that it is cryptographically secure when appropriate.
As of `rand` 0.7 / `rand_core` 0.5, implementations overriding this
method should ensure the implementation satisfies reproducibility
(in prior versions this was not required).

Fork this PRNG

This creates a new PRNG from the current one by initializing a new one and seeding it from the current one.

This is useful when initializing a PRNG for a thread

Fork this PRNG

This creates a new PRNG from the current one by initializing a new one and seeding it from the current one.

This is useful when initializing a PRNG for a thread.

This is the failable equivalent to `SeedableRng::fork`

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety", so this trait is not object safe.*

# TryCryptoRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/^0.10/trait.TryCryptoRng.html

`pub trait TryCryptoRng: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) { }## Expand description

A marker trait over [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) for securely unpredictable RNGs

This marker trait indicates that the implementing generator is intended, when correctly seeded and protected from side-channel attacks such as a leaking of state, to be a cryptographically secure generator. This trait is provided as a tool to aid review of cryptographic code, but does not by itself guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications.

Formally, a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator)
should satisfy an additional property over other generators: assuming that
the generator has been appropriately seeded and has unknown state, then
given the first *k* bits of an algorithm’s output
sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.

An optional property of CSPRNGs is backtracking resistance: if the CSPRNG’s
state is revealed, it will not be computationally-feasible to reconstruct
prior output values. This property is not required by `CryptoRng`.

Implementors of `TryCryptoRng` should only implement [ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) if a
default-constructed instance is itself a secure generator, for example

[which is a stateless interface.](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/struct.SysRng.html)

`getrandom::SysRng`

---

# rand_xorshift 0.5.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_xorshift/0.5.0

# rand_xorshift

Implements the Xorshift random number generator.

The Xorshift[^1] algorithm is not suitable for cryptographic purposes
but is very fast. If you do not know for sure that it fits your
requirements, use a more secure one such as `StdRng` or `OsRng`.

[^1]: Marsaglia, George (July 2003).
["Xorshift RNGs"](https://www.jstatsoft.org/v08/i14/paper).
*Journal of Statistical Software*. Vol. 8 (Issue 14).

Links:

## Crate Features

`rand_xorshift` is `no_std` compatible. It does not require any functionality
outside of the `core` lib, thus there are no features to configure.

The `serde` feature includes implementations of `Serialize` and `Deserialize`
for the included RNGs.

## License

`rand_xorshift` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.118/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# rand_xorshift - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_xorshift/0.5.0/target-redirect/rand_xorshift/

## Expand description

The xorshift random number generator.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

To initialize a generator, use the [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/seedable_rng/trait.SeedableRng.html) trait:

```
use rand_core::{SeedableRng, Rng};
use rand_xorshift::XorShiftRng;
let mut rng = XorShiftRng::seed_from_u64(0);
let x = rng.next_u32();
```

# XorShiftRng in rand_xorshift - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_xorshift/^0.5/struct.XorShiftRng.html

`pub struct XorShiftRng { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An Xorshift random number generator.

The Xorshift 1 algorithm is not suitable for cryptographic purposes
but is very fast. If you do not know for sure that it fits your
requirements, use a more secure one such as

`StdRng` or `OsRng`.When seeded with zero (i.e. `XorShiftRng::from_seed(0)` is called), this implementation
actually uses `0xBAD_5EED_0BAD_5EED_0BAD_5EED_0BAD_5EED` for the seed. This arbitrary value is
used because the underlying algorithm can’t escape from an all-zero state, and the function is
infallible so it can’t signal this by returning an error.

# subtle 2.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/2.6.1

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

```
 = "2.6"
```
This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and optimized back into a branch.

For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`'s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the *About* section below.

Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.

Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.

Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.

## Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

## Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.41** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

## About

This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.

Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
based on Tim Maclean's [work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security),
which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
software side-channels in Rust code.
From version

`2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels' work on
"Secret Types in Rust".`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.

## Warning

This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing cryptographic protocols. It represents a best-effort attempt to protect against some software side-channels. Because side-channel resistance is not a property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such effort is fundamentally limited.

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

---

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distributions](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type of random number generators

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait used to indicate that an `RngCore``BlockRngCore`
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Types which may be filled with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- An automatically-implemented extension trait on `RngCore`
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)
- The core of a random number generator.
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `std`and- `std_rng`
- Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)- rng - `std`and- `std_rng`
- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# Choice in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/^2.2.1/struct.Choice.html

`pub struct Choice(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

The `Choice` struct represents a choice for use in conditional assignment.

It is a wrapper around a `u8`, which should have the value either `1` (true)
or `0` (false).

The conversion from `u8` to `Choice` passes the value through an optimization
barrier, as a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from inferring that
the `Choice` value is a boolean. This strategy is based on Tim Maclean’s
[work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security), which attempts to provide
a more comprehensive approach for preventing software side-channels in Rust
code.

The `Choice` struct implements operators for AND, OR, XOR, and NOT, to allow
combining `Choice` values. These operations do not short-circuit.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#568-573)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Choice)### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#568-573)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Choice)

### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#119)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Copy-for-Choice)

Convert the `Choice` wrapper into a `bool`, depending on whether
the underlying `u8` was a `0` or a `1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#note-1)Note

This function exists to avoid having higher-level cryptographic protocol implementations duplicating this pattern.

The intended use case for this conversion is at the *end* of a
higher-level primitive implementation: for example, in checking a keyed
MAC, where the verification should happen in constant-time (and thus use
a `Choice`) but it is safe to return a `bool` at the end of the
verification.

# CtOption in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/^2.2.1/struct.CtOption.html

`pub struct CtOption<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `CtOption<T>` type represents an optional value similar to the
[ Option<T>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html) type but is intended for
use in constant time APIs.

Any given `CtOption<T>` is either `Some` or `None`, but unlike
`Option<T>` these variants are not exposed. The
[ is_some()](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.is_some) method is used to determine if
the value is

`Some`, and [and](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap_or)

`unwrap_or()`[methods are provided to access the underlying value. The value can also be obtained with](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap_or_else)

`unwrap_or_else()`[but this will panic if it is](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap)

`unwrap()``None`.Functions that are intended to be constant time may not produce
valid results for all inputs, such as square root and inversion
operations in finite field arithmetic. Returning an `Option<T>`
from these functions makes it difficult for the caller to reason
about the result in constant time, and returning an incorrect
value burdens the caller and increases the chance of bugs.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

This method is used to construct a new `CtOption<T>` and takes
a value of type `T`, and a `Choice` that determines whether
the optional value should be `Some` or not. If `is_some` is
false, the value will still be stored but its value is never
exposed.

This returns the underlying value if it is `Some`
or the provided value otherwise.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#722-728)#### pub fn [unwrap_or_else](https://docs.rs#method.unwrap_or_else)<F>(self, f: F) -> T

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#722-728)

#### pub fn [unwrap_or_else](https://docs.rs#method.unwrap_or_else)<F>(self, f: F) -> T

This returns the underlying value if it is `Some`
or the value produced by the provided closure otherwise.

This operates in constant time, because the provided closure is always called.

Returns a `None` value if the option is `None`, otherwise
returns a `CtOption` enclosing the value of the provided closure.
The closure is given the enclosed value or, if the option is
`None`, it is provided a dummy value computed using
`Default::default()`.

This operates in constant time, because the provided closure is always called.

Returns a `None` value if the option is `None`, otherwise
returns the result of the provided closure. The closure is
given the enclosed value or, if the option is `None`, it
is provided a dummy value computed using `Default::default()`.

This operates in constant time, because the provided closure is always called.

Returns `self` if it contains a value, and otherwise returns the result of
calling `f`. The provided function `f` is always called.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#815-817)#### pub fn [into_option](https://docs.rs#method.into_option)(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#815-817)

#### pub fn [into_option](https://docs.rs#method.into_option)(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>

Convert the `CtOption<T>` wrapper into an `Option<T>`, depending on whether
the underlying `is_some` `Choice` was a `0` or a `1` once unwrapped.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This function exists to avoid ending up with ugly, verbose and/or bad handled
conversions from the `CtOption<T>` wraps to an `Option<T>` or `Result<T, E>`.
This implementation doesn’t intend to be constant-time nor try to protect the
leakage of the `T` since the `Option<T>` will do it anyways.

It’s equivalent to the corresponding `From` impl, however this version is
friendlier for type inference.

# ConditionallySelectable in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/^2.2.1/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html

`pub trait ConditionallySelectable: `[Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [conditional_select](https://docs.rs#tymethod.conditional_select)(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) -> Self;
    // Provided methods
    fn [conditional_assign](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_assign)(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) { ... }
[conditional_swap](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_swap)(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) { ... }
}## Expand description

A type which can be conditionally selected in constant time.

This trait also provides generic implementations of conditional assignment and conditional swaps.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#420)#### fn [conditional_select](https://docs.rs#tymethod.conditional_select)(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#420)

#### fn [conditional_select](https://docs.rs#tymethod.conditional_select)(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) -> Self

Select `a` or `b` according to `choice`.

[§](https://docs.rs#returns)Returns

- `a`if- `choice == Choice(0)`;
- `b`if- `choice == Choice(1)`.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
let x: u8 = 13;
let y: u8 = 42;
let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 0.into());
assert_eq!(z, x);
let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 1.into());
assert_eq!(z, y);
```
## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#442-444)#### fn [conditional_assign](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_assign)(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#442-444)

#### fn [conditional_assign](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_assign)(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

Conditionally assign `other` to `self`, according to `choice`.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
let mut x: u8 = 13;
let mut y: u8 = 42;
x.conditional_assign(&y, 0.into());
assert_eq!(x, 13);
x.conditional_assign(&y, 1.into());
assert_eq!(x, 42);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#469-473)#### fn [conditional_swap](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_swap)(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#469-473)

#### fn [conditional_swap](https://docs.rs#method.conditional_swap)(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html))

Conditionally swap `self` and `other` if `choice == 1`; otherwise,
reassign both unto themselves.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
let mut x: u8 = 13;
let mut y: u8 = 42;
u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 0.into());
assert_eq!(x, 13);
assert_eq!(y, 42);
u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 1.into());
assert_eq!(x, 42);
assert_eq!(y, 13);
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#556-566)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Ordering)### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

`Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` where:

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#556-566)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Ordering)

### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

`Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` where:

- `Less`=> -1
- `Equal`=> 0
- `Greater`=> 1

Given this, it’s possible to operate on orderings as if they’re integers, which allows leveraging conditional masking for predication.

# ConstantTimeEq in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/^2.2.1/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html

```
pub trait ConstantTimeEq {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[ct_eq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.ct_eq)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html);
    // Provided method
    fn [ct_ne](https://docs.rs#method.ct_ne)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

An `Eq`-like trait that produces a `Choice` instead of a `bool`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
let x: u8 = 5;
let y: u8 = 13;
assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&y).unwrap_u8(), 0);
assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&x).unwrap_u8(), 1);
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#379-384)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConstantTimeEq-for-Ordering)### impl [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) for [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

`Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` making it possible to leverage `i8::ct_eq`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#379-384)

### impl [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) for [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

`Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` making it possible to leverage `i8::ct_eq`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#289-332)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConstantTimeEq-for-%5BT%5D)### impl<T: [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html)> [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) for [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#289-332)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConstantTimeEq-for-%5BT%5D)

### impl<T: [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html)> [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) for [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)

Check whether two slices of `ConstantTimeEq` types are equal.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This function short-circuits if the lengths of the input slices are different. Otherwise, it should execute in time independent of the slice contents.

Since arrays coerce to slices, this function works with fixed-size arrays:

```
let a: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7];
let b: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3];
let a_eq_a = a.ct_eq(&a);
let a_eq_b = a.ct_eq(&b);
assert_eq!(a_eq_a.unwrap_u8(), 1);
assert_eq!(a_eq_b.unwrap_u8(), 0);
```

# ConstantTimeGreater in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/^2.2.1/trait.ConstantTimeGreater.html

Trait ConstantTimeGreater    Copy item path  Source  ```
pub trait ConstantTimeGreater {
    // Required method
    fn
```
ct_gt (&self, other: &Self) -> Choice ;
}Expand description A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be greater
than another of the same type.

Determine whether `self > other`.

The bitwise-NOT of the return value of this function should be usable to
determine if `self <= other`.

This function should execute in constant time.

§ ReturnsA `Choice` with a set bit if `self > other`, and with no set bits
otherwise.

§ Exampleuse  subtle::ConstantTimeGreater;
let  x: u8 = 13 ;
let  y: u8 = 42 ;
let  x_gt_y = x.ct_gt(& y);
assert_eq! (x_gt_y.unwrap_u8(), 0 );
let  y_gt_x = y.ct_gt(& x);
assert_eq! (y_gt_x.unwrap_u8(), 1 );
let  x_gt_x = x.ct_gt(& x);
assert_eq! (x_gt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0 );This trait is not  dyn compatible .

In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".

Returns Choice::from(1) iff x > y, and Choice::from(0) iff x <= y.

§ NoteThis algoritm would also work for signed integers if we first
flip the top bit, e.g. `let x: u8 = x ^ 0x80`, etc.

Returns Choice::from(1) iff x > y, and Choice::from(0) iff x <= y.

§ NoteThis algoritm would also work for signed integers if we first
flip the top bit, e.g. `let x: u8 = x ^ 0x80`, etc.

# ConstantTimeLess in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/^2.2.1/trait.ConstantTimeLess.html

`pub trait ConstantTimeLess: `[ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) + [ConstantTimeGreater](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeGreater.html) {
    // Provided method
    fn [ct_lt](https://docs.rs#method.ct_lt)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be less than another of the same type.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Determine whether `self < other`.

The bitwise-NOT of the return value of this function should be usable to
determine if `self >= other`.

A default implementation is provided and implemented for the unsigned integer types.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#returns)Returns

A `Choice` with a set bit if `self < other`, and with no set bits
otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use subtle::ConstantTimeLess;
let x: u8 = 13;
let y: u8 = 42;
let x_lt_y = x.ct_lt(&y);
assert_eq!(x_lt_y.unwrap_u8(), 1);
let y_lt_x = y.ct_lt(&x);
assert_eq!(y_lt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
let x_lt_x = x.ct_lt(&x);
assert_eq!(x_lt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

[90](https://docs.rs#90)    /// the randomness required to sample an element. Implementors of `Group` must

[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// Efficient representation of an elliptic curve point.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)pub trait Curve: Group + GroupOps<Self::Affine> + GroupOpsOwned<Self::Affine> {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// The affine representation for this elliptic curve.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    type Affine: CurveAffine<Curve = Self, Scalar = Self::Scalar>;
[118](https://docs.rs#118)
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    /// Converts a batch of projective elements into affine elements. This function will
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    /// panic if `p.len() != q.len()`.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    fn batch_normalize(p: &[Self], q: &mut [Self::Affine]) {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)        assert_eq!(p.len(), q.len());
[123](https://docs.rs#123)
[124](https://docs.rs#124)        for (p, q) in p.iter().zip(q.iter_mut()) {
[125](https://docs.rs#125)            *q = p.to_affine();
[126](https://docs.rs#126)        }
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    }
[128](https://docs.rs#128)
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    /// Converts this element into its affine representation.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    fn to_affine(&self) -> Self::Affine;

[168](https://docs.rs#168)pub trait GroupEncoding: Sized {
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// The encoding of group elements.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    ///
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// The `Default` implementation is not required to return a valid point encoding. The
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// bound is present to enable encodings to be constructed generically:
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    /// ```
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// # use group::GroupEncoding;
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// # use subtle::CtOption;
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// # struct G;
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// # impl GroupEncoding for G {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// #     type Repr = [u8; 0];
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// #     fn from_bytes(bytes: &Self::Repr) -> CtOption<Self> { unimplemented!() }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// #     fn from_bytes_unchecked(bytes: &Self::Repr) -> CtOption<Self> { unimplemented!() }
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// #     fn to_bytes(&self) -> Self::Repr { unimplemented!() }
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// # }
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// # let buf = &[0u8; 0][..];
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// let mut encoding = <G as GroupEncoding>::Repr::default();
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// encoding.as_mut().copy_from_slice(buf);
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// ```
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    ///
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    /// It is recommended that the default should be the all-zeroes encoding.
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    type Repr: Copy + Default + Send + Sync + 'static + AsRef<[u8]> + AsMut<[u8]>;
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// Attempts to deserialize a group element from its encoding.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    fn from_bytes(bytes: &Self::Repr) -> CtOption<Self>;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    /// Attempts to deserialize a group element, not checking if the element is valid.
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    ///
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// **This is dangerous to call unless you trust the bytes you are reading; otherwise,
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    /// API invariants may be broken.** Please consider using
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// [`GroupEncoding::from_bytes`] instead.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    fn from_bytes_unchecked(bytes: &Self::Repr) -> CtOption<Self>;
[200](https://docs.rs#200)
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// Converts this element into its byte encoding. This may or may not support
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// encoding the identity.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    // TODO: Figure out how to handle identity encoding generically.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    fn to_bytes(&self) -> Self::Repr;
[205](https://docs.rs#205)}
[206](https://docs.rs#206)

# Wnaf in group - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/group/latest/target-redirect/group/struct.Wnaf.html

`pub struct Wnaf<W, B, S> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A “w-ary non-adjacent form” scalar multiplication (also known as exponentiation) context.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This struct can be used to implement several patterns:

[§](https://docs.rs#one-base-one-scalar)One base, one scalar

For this pattern, you can use a transient `Wnaf` context:

[§](https://docs.rs#many-bases-one-scalar)Many bases, one scalar

For this pattern, you create a `Wnaf` context, load the scalar into it, and then
process each base in turn:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use group::Wnaf;
let mut wnaf = Wnaf::new();
let mut wnaf_scalar = wnaf.scalar(&scalar);
let results: Vec<_> = bases
    .into_iter()
    .map(|base| wnaf_scalar.base(base))
    .collect();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#one-base-many-scalars)One base, many scalars

For this pattern, you create a `Wnaf` context, load the base into it, and then process
each scalar in turn:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use group::Wnaf;
let mut wnaf = Wnaf::new();
let mut wnaf_base = wnaf.base(base, scalars.len());
let results: Vec<_> = scalars
    .iter()
    .map(|scalar| wnaf_base.scalar(scalar))
    .collect();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#many-bases-many-scalars)Many bases, many scalars

Say you have `n` bases and `m` scalars, and want to produce `n * m` results. For this
pattern, you need to cache the w-NAF tables for the bases and then compute the w-NAF
form of the scalars on the fly for every base, or vice versa:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use group::Wnaf;
let mut wnaf_contexts: Vec<_> = (0..bases.len()).map(|_| Wnaf::new()).collect();
let mut wnaf_bases: Vec<_> = wnaf_contexts
    .iter_mut()
    .zip(bases)
    .map(|(wnaf, base)| wnaf.base(base, scalars.len()))
    .collect();
let results: Vec<_> = wnaf_bases
    .iter()
    .flat_map(|wnaf_base| scalars.iter().map(|scalar| wnaf_base.scalar(scalar)))
    .collect();
```
Alternatively, use the [ WnafBase](https://docs.rs/struct.WnafBase.html) and

[types, which enable the various tables and w-NAF forms to be cached individually per base and scalar. These types can then be directly multiplied without any additional runtime work, at the cost of fixing a specific window size (rather than choosing the window size dynamically).](https://docs.rs/struct.WnafScalar.html)

`WnafScalar`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Constructs new space for the scalar representation while borrowing the computed window table, for sending the window table across threads.

Constructs new space for the window table while borrowing the computed scalar representation, for sending the scalar representation across threads.

# WnafBase in group - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/group/latest/target-redirect/group/struct.WnafBase.html

## Expand description

A fixed window table for a group element, precomputed to improve the speed of scalar multiplication.

This struct is designed for usage patterns that have long-term cached bases and/or
scalars, or [Cartesian products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product) of bases and scalars. The [ Wnaf](https://docs.rs/struct.Wnaf.html) API enables one or
the other to be cached, but requires either the base window tables or the scalar w-NAF
forms to be computed repeatedly on the fly, which can become a significant performance
issue for some use cases.

`WnafBase` and [ WnafScalar](https://docs.rs/struct.WnafScalar.html) enable an alternative trade-off: by fixing the window
size at compile time, the precomputations are guaranteed to only occur once per base
and once per scalar. Users should select their window size based on how long the bases
are expected to live; a larger window size will consume more memory and take longer to
precompute, but result in faster scalar multiplications.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use group::{WnafBase, WnafScalar};
let wnaf_bases: Vec<_> = bases.into_iter().map(WnafBase::<_, 4>::new).collect();
let wnaf_scalars: Vec<_> = scalars.iter().map(WnafScalar::new).collect();
let results: Vec<_> = wnaf_bases
    .iter()
    .flat_map(|base| wnaf_scalars.iter().map(|scalar| base * scalar))
    .collect();
```
Note that this pattern requires specifying a fixed window size (unlike previous
patterns that picked a suitable window size internally). This is necessary to ensure
in the type system that the base and scalar `Wnaf`s were computed with the same window
size, allowing the result to be computed infallibly.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

}## Expand description

This trait represents an element of a cryptographic group.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Returns an element chosen uniformly at random from the non-identity elements of this group using a user-provided fallible RNG.

Returns `Err` propagating the RNG’s error if the underlying RNG fails to produce
the randomness required to sample an element. Implementors of `Group` must
provide this method; [ Group::random](https://docs.rs/trait.Group.html#method.random) is derived from it for infallible RNGs.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Returns an element chosen uniformly at random from the non-identity elements of this group using a user-provided infallible RNG.

This is a convenience wrapper around [ Group::try_random](https://docs.rs/trait.Group.html#tymethod.try_random) for RNGs that cannot
fail. Use

[if your RNG may fail (for example, an OS-backed entropy source).](https://docs.rs/trait.Group.html#tymethod.try_random)

`Group::try_random`## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

}## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

The encoding of group elements.

The `Default` implementation is not required to return a valid point encoding. The
bound is present to enable encodings to be constructed generically:

```
let mut encoding = <G as GroupEncoding>::Repr::default();
encoding.as_mut().copy_from_slice(buf);
```
It is recommended that the default should be the all-zeroes encoding.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap::Command

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`
